characterList.name: Scott Henderson

characterList.description: A middle-aged man with short brown hair and a goatee, wearing a blue checkered shirt, blue jeans, and a gray flat cap. He's asking questions about the RC Booster pedal.
characterList.name: Interviewer

content_metadata.description: An informative interview with guitarist Scott Henderson about the Xotic Effects RC-Booster SH Limited pedal.

qAndA.answer: He emphasizes its 'transparency,' meaning it boosts the existing signal without adding its own distinct color or distortion.
qAndA.question: How does Scott Henderson describe the sound of the original RC Booster?

qAndA.answer: He used a Tube Screamer and a Voodoo 1 pedal. The Tube Screamer provided the gain, and the Voodoo 1, being a scooped pedal, helped to cut out the mid-range frequencies he disliked.
qAndA.question: What two pedals did Scott Henderson combine to achieve a similar effect to the RC Booster before its existence?

qAndA.answer: He particularly likes the bass and treble knobs, which allow him to fine-tune the low and high-end frequencies of his sound.
qAndA.question: What specific feature of the RC Booster does Scott Henderson appreciate for shaping his tone?

qAndA.answer: The new version allows him to achieve both a good lead sound and a clean sound without significantly adjusting his guitar volume. It provides more control and dynamic range for his playing style.
qAndA.question: Why does Scott Henderson prefer the new dual-channel RC Booster over the original?

qAndA.answer: He uses an SVC (short for 'Smart Volume Control') pedal in the effects loop of his amplifier. This allows him to adjust the overall volume without altering the amount of gain from the RC Booster.
qAndA.question: How does Scott Henderson control his overall volume when using the RC Booster?

narrativeProgression.description: The interview begins with a question about Scott Henderson's long-time use of the RC Booster pedal.
Scott emphasizes the pedal's transparency and how it boosts the amp's sound without adding color.
He describes a previous setup combining a Tube Screamer and a Voodoo 1 to achieve a similar effect.
He explains how the RC Booster's bass and treble knobs allow for tonal shaping.
The discussion shifts to how Scott uses the pedal, mainly for a boosted blues lead sound.
He mentions using a separate distortion pedal for a more extreme gain.
The conversation moves to the new dual-channel RC Booster and its differences.
Scott explains his preference for the new dual-channel model for its improved clean sound and volume control.
They discuss Scott's philosophy of driving the amp's front end with the pedal.
He explains how he uses an SVC pedal in the effects loop to control master volume without affecting gain.

text_to_speech: Ok, so the RC Booster. It's been in your pedalboard for many years. What was the initial attraction to this pedal and how does it compliment your tone? Well, first of all it's really transparent. That's the thing I care about the most. I just want more from the amp but I don't want color. Because the colors comes from the guitar and the amp. And the RC Booster doesn't really have a sound of it's own. It just boosts what's there. And before that existed... I don't think there was anything that I was happy with. I was using lots of stuff. I was trying to use the Tube Screamer... Because that has about the same amount of gain. But it's got a huge mid-range peak which I didn't like. And especially for the treble pickup. And I tried combining that with the Voodoo-1. I'd put the Tube Screamer into the Voodoo-1. And Voodoo-1 being a very scooped pedal... It would kind of get rid of the Tube Screamer's mid-range hump. And that's what I used mainly on the "Well to the Bone" album. Because there wasn't RC Booster back then. When this came along... I didn't have to use the combination of those pedals anymore. I could just use one pedal and I just love the sound it. It's killer because it has treble and bass knobs on it. Which let's you... I like to take a little bit of the bass out. So that the cords are cleaner and aren't muddy. And that also helps actually with the solos too, with the gain. So that leads me into my next question which is... Lot of guys, some guys leave the boost on all the time and then add to it. And some guys use the boost just for solos. How do you use this booster? I just have it on when I'm using it by itself. In other words, for a boosted tone which is more like a blues lead sound. It's on. Then if I want more gainy type of legato, horn like sound... I use another distortion pedal and turn the RC Booster off. I don't combined pedals because it's a little noisy for me. There's a little too much hiss when I combine pedals. The only time I would do it is... I would combine the RC Booster with my distortion pedal to... just get a completely over the top, nuts, haywire, out of control sound. That's just to make noise. Do you find that with the knobs... you set them at 12 o'clock? Or are gain, volume, treble and bass at different areas? They're at different areas. Just depends on the pedal. I set the... because the new RC Booster... The 2 channel one is a completely different animal than the first one. You set the two gain knobs so that you get a good lead sound... and good clean sound when you switch between channels. So I would set that up a little bit differently. Though the bass and treble knobs are pretty much the same on both. So let's talk about the new one. Did you have a lot of input on how it was designed? Or did you kind of say "Hey, I need this if you guys are..." I basically just asked Kiyoshi to make RC Booster with two different gain stages. Because normally, as most guys do that play one channel amps... You would use your boost pedal on with your guitar up pretty high... to get a lead sound and then turn the guitar down to play cords. And what I was finding is that... The RC Booster cleans up really nice when you turned down to play chords. More than most boost pedals but I was having to turn down my guitar... too far to get it clean. Right? And by the time I got it completely clean, it was too soft. The volume was too soft and then I have to turn up my master volume overall. With the new pedal, I can leave my guitar pretty much where it is. I can leave it on around 9 for solos turn it down to about 7 or 8 for chords. And the chords sound is much bigger, much cleaner, there's not as much treble loss. And everything just sounds better. Now, the new pedal that you've had a chance to use it... does it work well with other pedals as well in your pedal board? Well, I don't combine pedals but it's matched tonally very well... to the rest of my pedals as far as... I'm able to get the treble and bass of all my pedals in the same range. So that when I hit one pedal as opposed another when... it doesn't super increase in the brightness or the bass. Except for the Fuzz Factory. Fuzz Factory just has a ton of bass so as soon as you turn it on... it's like all this low end... but that's just the nature that pedal. I guess I was thinking about it and maybe your philosophy is... You kind of pummel the front end of the amp. And that kind of keeps... preserves the amp's tone. A lot of people ask me... "If you want a cleaner tone, why don't you just turn off the pedal?" Well, the reason is because, to really use a pedal, I think, like the RC Booster... the volume is to be all the way up. It really needs to kick the front end of the preamp of the amp. So if you're doing that, and then you turn the pedal off, you've got nothing The difference between volume is just huge. So I understand now. So you pummel that but then you cut back on your volume. And that can kind of clean up your tone a little. And I've got a volume in the effects loop of the amp. One of those SVC pedals. (Subtle Volume Control) So I'm using the SVC pedal in the effects loop control my master volume... without affecting the gain and then I'm using the guitar to to set the gain. How much or how little gain there is. So I've got two controls. On the guitar for the gain and on the floor for the overall volume. And like that because the music we're playing is pretty dynamic So there is a lot of times I have to play with pretty overdriven tone... but not a really loud volume. So I can turn my guitar up and then turn the volume down. Or if I want a super clean, loud clean sound... I just jack the volume all the way up on the floor and turn my guitar down and get... a really super clean sound or I can even turn the pedal off completely, If I want a very very clean guitar sound. Sometimes I use multi-tap delays to make that kind of... Holdsworth sound type of swells, you know. And that actually sounds better with no pedals at all. Just completely clean. And that I can just jack the volume on the floor all the way up for that sound. What kind of amps you think this pedal is going to work well with? Would you say mostly a clean amp, Fender style or any type of amp? Well, any amp really but it needs to be set a little crunchy. Pedals don't sound very good when the amp is completely clean. It sounds a little thin. You need the amp tubes to be working a little bit. It's really like... probably about 25% from the amp and 75% from the pedal. If the app is completely clean, then it just doesn't feel right. The amp is not working hard enough. So the amp is crunchy and let the pedals do the rest. That seems to be the fattest sound to me. Great.
